hints: Focus on whether each reaction would need heat supplied to keep going, or would give out heat by itself.
Notice that neutralisation, making a bond from atoms, and burning a metal in oxygen are all classic heat-releasing processes.
Look for the reaction that breaks a very stable solid apart into two products, the one you have to heat strongly in a kiln.
walkthrough:
**Recall what endothermic means**

Endothermic means heat energy is taken in from the surroundings, so $\Delta H$ is positive. Exothermic means heat is given out, so $\Delta H$ is negative.

$$\text{endothermic: heat in, } \Delta H > 0$$

**Sort the familiar exothermic types**

Neutralisation (acid + base), bond formation from gaseous atoms, and combustion or oxidation of a metal all release energy and feel hot. That covers three of the reactions here.

**Spot the thermal decomposition**

Breaking $\text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)}$ into $\text{CaO(s)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$ needs continuous strong heating to break ionic bonds and make a gas. That constant need for heat is the sign of an endothermic reaction.

$$\text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)} \rightarrow \text{CaO(s)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$$

options.A: This is a neutralisation between $\text{Ca(OH)}_2\text{(aq)}$ and $\text{HCl(aq)}$. Formation of water from $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ releases heat, so it is exothermic, not endothermic.
options.B: This shows two $\text{Cl(g)}$ atoms joining to form a $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond in $\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)}$. Bond formation always releases energy, so it is exothermic.
options.C: This is oxidation or combustion of calcium metal to form $\text{CaO(s)}$. Burning metals in oxygen releases a lot of heat and light, so it is strongly exothermic.
options.D: This is thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate. It requires strong, continuous heating to break down the lattice and release $\text{CO}_2$, so heat is absorbed and the reaction is endothermic.
